arrays.name: Arrays
arrays.description: A data structure that stores elements in contiguous memory, allowing for O(1) access by index.

linked_lists.name: Linked Lists
linked_lists.description: A linear data structure where each node points to the next node in the sequence.

stacks_and_queues.name: Stacks and Queues
stacks_and_queues.description: Linear data structures that manage elements according to Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) or First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principles.

recursion.name: Recursion
recursion.description: A programming technique where a function calls itself to process smaller instances of the same problem.

sorting.name: Sorting Algorithms
sorting.description: Algorithms such as Quicksort and Merge sort that arrange data in a specific order, with varying time and space complexities.

binary_search.name: Binary Search
binary_search.description: An algorithm that finds an item in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search interval.

hashing.name: Hashing
hashing.description: A technique that maps keys to specific indices in a table using a hash function for fast data retrieval.

trees.name: Trees
trees.description: Non-linear hierarchical data structures where each node has a parent and zero or more children, such as Binary Search Trees.

heaps.name: Heaps
heaps.description: Special tree data structures used to efficiently implement priority queues with O(log n) insert and extract operations.

graphs.name: Graph Algorithms
graphs.description: Structures of nodes (vertices) and edges used to model relationships, with traversal algorithms like BFS and DFS.

shortest_paths.name: Shortest Path Algorithms
shortest_paths.description: Algorithms like Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford that find the lowest-cost path between nodes in a weighted graph.

dynamic_programming.name: Dynamic Programming
dynamic_programming.description: A method for solving complex problems by breaking them down into overlapping subproblems and reusing stored solutions.

array_techniques.name: Array and String Techniques
array_techniques.description: Optimization strategies like sliding windows and two pointers to process arrays more efficiently in O(n) time.

complexity_analysis.name: Complexity Analysis
complexity_analysis.description: The mathematical study of how an algorithm's time and space requirements grow relative to the input size using Big-O notation.

JD: Software Engineer (New Grad), Product Company

claims.statement: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, which allows any element to be accessed in O(1) time.
claims.quote: An array stores elements in contiguous memory, so any element can be accessed by index in O(1) time.

claims.statement: Inserting or deleting an element in the middle of an array takes O(n) time because existing elements must be shifted.
claims.quote: Inserting or deleting in the middle of an array takes O(n) time because elements must be shifted.

claims.statement: Big-O notation describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the input size n increases.
claims.quote: Big-O notation describes how the running time grows as the input size n grows.

claims.statement: Inserting an element at the head of a linked list is an O(1) operation.
claims.quote: Inserting at the head of a linked list takes O(1) time, but accessing the k-th element takes O(k)

claims.statement: A stack follows Last In First Out (LIFO) order, meaning the most recently added item is the first to be removed.
claims.quote: A stack follows Last In First Out (LIFO) order, with push and pop at the top.

claims.statement: A queue operates on a First In First Out (FIFO) basis, adding elements at the rear and removing them from the front.
claims.quote: A queue follows First In First Out (FIFO) order, adding at the rear and removing from the front.

claims.statement: A recursive function must call itself on a smaller input and include a base case to stop the infinite loop.
claims.quote: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and must have a base case to stop.

claims.statement: Each recursive call requires stack space, meaning that very deep recursion can lead to a stack overflow error.
claims.quote: Each recursive call uses stack space, so very deep recursion can cause a stack overflow.

claims.statement: Bubble sort and insertion sort have a worst-case time complexity of O(n^2).
claims.quote: Bubble sort and insertion sort take O(n^2) time in the worst case.

claims.statement: Merge sort divides the array into halves, sorts them, and merges them, guaranteeing O(n log n) time in all cases.
claims.quote: Merge sort divides the array into halves, sorts them and merges them, taking O(n log n) time in all cases.

claims.statement: Quicksort has an average time complexity of O(n log n) but degrades to O(n^2) in the worst case if the pivot is chosen badly.
claims.quote: Quicksort takes O(n log n) time on average, but O(n^2) in the worst case when the pivot is chosen badly.

claims.statement: Binary search requires a sorted array and repeatedly halves the search range, resulting in O(log n) time complexity.
claims.quote: Binary search works only on a sorted array and repeatedly halves the search range, taking O(log n) time.

claims.statement: A hash table maps keys to values using a hash function that computes an array index.
claims.quote: A hash table maps keys to values using a hash function to compute an index.

claims.statement: Python dictionaries do not preserve insertion order, so one should not rely on the order of keys when iterating.
claims.quote: Python dictionaries are hash tables, and Python dictionaries do not preserve insertion order, so never rely on the order of keys when iterating.

claims.statement: A binary tree is a tree structure where every node has a maximum of two children.
claims.quote: A binary tree is a tree in which every node has at most two children.

claims.statement: In a binary search tree, the left subtree contains smaller keys and the right contains larger keys, meaning an inorder traversal yields sorted order.
claims.quote: In a binary search tree, the left subtree holds smaller keys and the right subtree holds larger keys, so an inorder traversal visits keys in sorted order.

claims.statement: Searching a binary search tree takes O(h) time, where h represents the height of the tree.
claims.quote: Searching a binary search tree takes O(h) time, where h is the height of the tree.

claims.statement: A binary heap is a complete binary tree that implements a priority queue with O(log n) time for insert and extract-min operations.
claims.quote: A binary heap is a complete binary tree used to implement a priority queue, with insert and extract-min in O(log n) time.

claims.statement: Graphs can be stored as adjacency matrices or lists, with adjacency lists being more memory efficient for sparse graphs.
claims.quote: A graph can be stored as an adjacency matrix or an adjacency list; adjacency lists use less memory for sparse graphs.

claims.statement: Breadth-first search (BFS) utilizes a queue and is used to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
claims.quote: Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

claims.statement: Depth-first search (DFS) utilizes a stack or recursion and is commonly used for cycle detection and topological sorting.
claims.quote: Depth-first search (DFS) uses a stack or recursion and is used for cycle detection and topological sorting.

claims.statement: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source node but requires all edge weights to be non-negative.
claims.quote: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source but requires all edge weights to be non-negative.

claims.statement: The Bellman-Ford algorithm should be used when a graph contains negative edge weights.
claims.quote: When a graph has negative edge weights, use the Bellman-Ford algorithm instead.

claims.statement: Appending to a dynamic array takes amortized O(1) time because the array occasionally doubles its capacity.
claims.quote: Appending to a dynamic array takes amortized O(1) time, because the array occasionally doubles its capacity.

claims.statement: A hash table provides O(1) lookup on average, but its worst case is O(n) when many keys collide into the same bucket.
claims.quote: A hash table gives O(1) lookup on average, but the worst case is O(n) when many keys collide into the same bucket.

claims.statement: Since Python 3.7, dictionaries are guaranteed to preserve insertion order as part of the language specification.
claims.quote: Since Python 3.7, dictionaries are guaranteed to preserve insertion order as part of the language specification.

claims.statement: Python's built-in sort algorithm uses Timsort, which is a stable algorithm that runs in O(n log n) time in the worst case.
claims.quote: Python's built-in sort uses Timsort, which is stable and runs in O(n log n) time in the worst case.

claims.statement: Quicksort degrades to O(n^2) time complexity on already sorted input when the first element is always chosen as the pivot.
claims.quote: Quicksort degrades to O(n^2) on already sorted input when the first element is always chosen as the pivot

claims.statement: Merge sort is stable and guarantees O(n log n), while quicksort is often faster in practice due to cache behavior, meaning neither is always faster.
claims.quote: Merge sort is stable and guarantees O(n log n), while quicksort is often faster in practice because of cache behaviour, so neither is always faster.

claims.statement: Using a binary heap, Dijkstra's algorithm runs in O((V + E) log V) time and is only correct when all edge weights are non-negative.
claims.quote: Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap runs in O((V + E) log V) time and is only correct when every edge weight is non-negative.

claims.statement: The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles negative edge weights in O(V * E) time and can also detect negative cycles in a graph.
claims.quote: The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles negative edge weights in O(V * E) time and can also detect negative cycles.

claims.statement: Dynamic programming solves problems that exhibit overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
claims.quote: Dynamic programming solves problems that have overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.

claims.statement: Memoization stores results of recursive calls in a top-down manner, while tabulation fills a table in a bottom-up manner.
claims.quote: Memoization stores the results of recursive calls top-down, while tabulation fills a table bottom-up.

claims.statement: The 0/1 knapsack problem and the longest common subsequence problem are considered classic examples of dynamic programming.
claims.quote: The 0/1 knapsack problem and the longest common subsequence problem are classic dynamic programming examples.

claims.statement: The sliding window technique maintains a moving range over an array to solve subarray problems in O(n) time instead of O(n^2).
claims.quote: The sliding window technique keeps a moving range over an array to solve subarray problems in O(n) time instead of O(n^2).

claims.statement: The two pointers technique moves two indices through a sorted array to find specific pairs, such as those with a given sum, in O(n) time.
claims.quote: The two pointers technique moves two indices through a sorted array, for example to find a pair with a given sum in O(n) time.

claims.statement: Hash table lookup is always O(1) regardless of the keys that are inserted into the table.
claims.quote: Hash table lookup is always O(1), no matter what keys you insert.

claims.statement: Quicksort is always faster than merge sort and should be used in all interview settings.
claims.quote: Quicksort is always faster than merge sort, so always use quicksort in interviews.

claims.statement: Dijkstra's algorithm can handle negative edge weights as long as the graph does not contain a negative cycle.
claims.quote: Dijkstra's algorithm works fine with negative edge weights as long as the graph has no negative cycle.

claims.statement: Recursive solutions are always slower than iterative ones and should be avoided in coding interviews.
claims.quote: Recursion is always slower than iteration, so avoid recursive solutions in coding interviews.

claims.statement: Candidates for a product company software engineer role must have strong problem-solving skills involving arrays, strings, hashing, and trees.
claims.quote: Strong problem solving with arrays, strings, hashing and trees.

claims.statement: A product company software engineer must know graph algorithms including BFS, DFS, and shortest paths.
claims.quote: Graph algorithms including BFS, DFS and shortest paths.

claims.statement: Candidates must apply dynamic programming to solve optimization problems for a product company role.
claims.quote: Dynamic programming for optimisation problems.

claims.statement: Job applicants need to use sliding window and two pointers techniques for efficient array and string processing.
claims.quote: Sliding window and two pointers techniques for efficient array and string processing.

claims.statement: Software engineers must be able to analyze time and space complexity using Big-O notation.
claims.quote: Ability to analyse time and space complexity using Big-O notation.

claims.statement: Candidates are expected to have experience in Python, Java, or C++, as well as familiarity with Git.
claims.quote: Experience in Python, Java or C++ and familiarity with Git.

claims.statement: A backend engineer for a fintech company must use heaps and priority queues for scheduling payment retries.
claims.quote: Heaps and priority queues for scheduling payment retries.

claims.statement: Backend engineers must use hash maps for fast lookups, utilizing Python dictionaries' insertion order preservation for ordered event processing.
claims.quote: Hash maps for fast lookups, and Python dictionaries, which preserve insertion order, for ordered event processing.

claims.statement: Candidates need dynamic programming and graph algorithms skills to handle fraud detection and routing problems in fintech.
claims.quote: Dynamic programming and graph algorithms for fraud detection and routing problems.

claims.statement: Fintech backend engineers must have a clear understanding of time and space complexity.
claims.quote: Clear understanding of time and space complexity.

conflicts.summary: The web cheatsheet claims hash lookups are always O(1), while the textbook notes the worst case is O(n) when collisions occur.

sides.label: Hash table lookup is always O(1) regardless of keys
Hash table worst-case lookup is O(n) due to collisions

conflicts.explanation: Trusted "Hash table worst-case lookup is O(n) due to collisions" over "Hash table lookup is always O(1) regardless of keys" because of: newer source (2024 vs 2015), higher-authority source, more specific (gives versions or reasons), the other side makes an absolute 'always/never' claim.

conflicts.summary: The 2016 faculty notes state Python dictionaries do not preserve insertion order, but the 2024 textbook and current job descriptions confirm that since Python 3.7 they do.
